messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Urban Planner
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 77

The rain comes down hard the night it happens. Amari is twenty-three, walking home from a late shift, taking a shortcut through the underpass near the old transit hub. He learned to navigate these streets from his father in Lagos, who taught him to read alleyways like weather patterns. That night, three men step out from behind a rusted dumpster. The first punch catches him in the ribs. The second sends his glasses skidding across wet pavement. He curls into himself, counting the flickering streetlights overhead, trying to memorize the cadence of their voices. When they leave, he stays on the ground for a long time, listening to the hum of the city he’s supposed to understand, until his legs finally remember how to work. He wakes up in the same bed three years later, but the ceiling fan sounds like the rumble of the transport van that took him to the hospital. His chest tightens before he even opens his eyes. At his desk, his third-floor office overlooks a grid of downtown streets he helped design. Now, the map feels like a trap. He traces the blue lines of planned walkways with his finger, but his mind jumps to the concrete of the underpass, the angle of the dumpster, the way the shadow fell. He cancels site visits. He tells his supervisor he has deadlines to meet, but he’s sitting in his apartment, watching traffic cameras on his monitor, waiting for someone to knock. When the building intercom buzzes, he doesn’t answer. He just presses his palms flat against his thighs until his breathing evens out. His work demands he see cities as living systems—rivers of traffic, nodes of community, pathways of safety. Now, he sees only threats. During a zoning committee meeting last week, a man in the back row stood up too quickly. Amari’s jaw locked. His breath shallowed. He excused himself without a word, walking out into the parking garage where the fluorescent lights hummed at the same frequency as the night of the assault. He stands by his car, eyes fixed on the reflection in the side mirror, watching the alley between two sedans. He tells himself he’s just being practical when he checks the corners, when he refuses to sit in the middle seat, when he stops going to the neighborhood gym and starts walking only on wide, well-lit boulevards where he can see three blocks ahead. In my office, he sits near the door. When he speaks, his voice stays level, but his shoulders hike toward his ears. He describes his nightmares not as stories, but as sensations: the taste of copper, the weight of a knee on his spine, the sudden silence after the shouting. He says he used to love walking through neighborhoods he was planning to revitalize. Now, he scrolls through satellite imagery instead, tracing property lines from a safe distance. His phone buzzes with messages from friends asking if he’s okay. He reads them, types a reply, then deletes it. He doesn’t want to explain why he flinches when a door slams, why he sleeps with his back to the wall, why he watches his own reflection in the window and sometimes doesn’t recognize the man staring back. He opens the file on his lap, draws a clean boundary line around a vacant lot, and asks if this block still makes sense. I watch his pen hover over the paper, then set it down. We sit in the quiet, mapping nothing at all.
